subjects.title: CCAF 2 - Claude Code
subjects.description: Domain 2 (20%) - CLAUDE.md hierarchy, slash commands, hooks, permissions, headless mode, and CI/CD integration.

cards.question: Three MCP tools return dates as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, and numeric codes, and the agent keeps comparing them wrongly. What is the cleanest fix?
cards.answer: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results for transformation before the model sees them (the SDK hook can replace the output with `updatedToolOutput`), which is exactly the named use case for normalizing heterogeneous formats. Rewriting third-party servers is often not an option; prompting makes the model do conversions it should never have been handed.

choices.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that normalizes each tool's result before the model processes it
A system prompt section explaining each tool's date format and how to convert
Few-shot examples showing correct date comparisons across all three of the tool formats
A rewrite of all three MCP servers so each emits ISO 8601 timestamps

hints: Fix it once on the way in, or explain it forever in the prompt?

cards.question: You have a user `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and a project `./CLAUDE.md`. How does Claude Code combine them?
cards.answer: Both are concatenated into context, ordered from broad to specific, so the project file appears after the user file. They do not override each other the way settings files do. If they conflict, Claude may follow either one, so keep them consistent.

choices.text: Both load; the project file appears later in context than the user file
The project file replaces the user file entirely for work in this repository
The user file wins, because user-level configuration outranks project scope
Only the file nearest the working directory loads; the other is ignored entirely

hints: Do CLAUDE.md files replace one another, or pile up?

cards.question: A CI job must have Claude review every PR and emit machine-readable output for a downstream step. What is the right invocation?
cards.answer: Headless mode with `--print` and `--output-format json` gives a single structured result object the next step can parse. The `@claude` mention flow is interactive and only fires when a human writes a comment.

choices.text: `claude -p "..." --output-format json` with an explicit `--allowedTools` list
An interactive `claude` session left running inside the CI runner
Post an `@claude` comment from the workflow and wait for it
`claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` so no permission prompt blocks the run

hints: "Every PR" eliminates one option; "machine-readable" eliminates another.

cards.question: Where do you put an MCP server config so the whole team gets it from version control?
cards.answer: `.mcp.json` at the repository root is the project scope - committed and shared. In interactive sessions, Claude Code asks for approval before using servers defined there, since other people wrote that config.

choices.text: `.mcp.json` at the repository root
`~/.claude/settings.json`
`.claude/settings.local.json`
`CLAUDE.md`, as a documented setup step

hints: Version control means a committed file - and this one does not live inside .claude/.

cards.question: A file at `.claude/commands/deploy/staging.md` creates which slash command?
cards.answer: `/deploy:staging` - subdirectories namespace commands, and the filename is the command name.

choices.text: `/deploy:staging`
`/staging`
`/deploy/staging`
`/deploy staging`

hints: Subdirectories do something specific to the command name.

cards.question: Which skill frontmatter field prompts the developer for a parameter when the skill is invoked bare?
cards.answer: `argument-hint` shows the expected arguments (for example `[issue-number]`), so a developer knows what to pass. `allowed-tools` controls tool access, `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated subagent, and `description` tells Claude when to use it. Note: current docs describe `argument-hint` as a hint shown during autocomplete and `allowed-tools` as pre-approving tools rather than restricting them; the exam guide's wording is kept here.

choices.text: `argument-hint`
`allowed-tools`
`context: fork`
`description`

hints: Three of these control how or when the skill runs; only one is about its input.

cards.question: Your CLAUDE.md is too long. Which change actually reduces the context it consumes?
cards.answer: Path-scoped rules load only when Claude works with matching files, so they genuinely cut startup context. `@` imports are expanded and loaded at launch, and `CLAUDE.local.md` and the user file also load at startup, so those only move the text around. (Block-level HTML comments are stripped too, but only use them for notes meant for humans.)

choices.text: Move sections into `.claude/rules/` files with `paths` frontmatter
Split it into several files pulled in with `@path` imports
Move the content into `CLAUDE.local.md`
Move the long sections into your user `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`

hints: Which option actually loads less at startup, rather than just reorganizing the files?

cards.question: What is the most important field in a custom subagent definition for getting it used at the right time?
cards.answer: `description`. The main agent reads it to decide whether to delegate, so it should read as a trigger condition ("use after changes to auth or input handling"), not as a title.

choices.text: `description` - it is what the main agent matches against to decide when to delegate
`model` - a stronger model makes the main agent pick the subagent more often
`name` - the main agent matches the task against the subagent's name
`tools` - without an explicit tool list the subagent cannot act on anything at all

hints: The main agent has to decide to delegate. What does it read in order to decide?

cards.question: A new team member cloned the repo today, but their Claude ignores conventions that everyone else's Claude follows. What is the likely cause?
cards.answer: User-level settings apply only to that user: instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are not shared with teammates through version control. The fix is to move them to the project CLAUDE.md (or .claude/rules/), which everyone gets when they clone.

choices.text: The instructions sit in user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is not shared through git
The conventions sit in `.claude/rules/`, which loads only for the person who wrote them
The project `CLAUDE.md` is too long, so Claude drops the conventions near its end
Their Claude Code version predates the configuration hierarchy the team relies on

hints: Whose machine is that file on?

cards.question: A monorepo has eight packages with different standards, and one CLAUDE.md is becoming unmanageable. What keeps it modular?
cards.answer: The @import syntax references external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular - selectively including the standards files relevant to each package. Duplication drifts; prefixing keeps everything loaded for everyone. Note: current Claude Code docs write this as `@path/to/file` (no literal `import` keyword), and imported files load at launch, so imports help organization but do not reduce context.

choices.text: Use `@import` so each package's CLAUDE.md pulls in only the standards files it needs
Duplicate the relevant sections into a CLAUDE.md inside each of the eight packages
Keep one CLAUDE.md and prefix each rule with the package name it applies to
Move all eight sets of standards into skills, invoked per package on demand

hints: Each standard should live in one place, and each package picks its own set.

cards.question: Terraform files are spread across many directories, and their conventions should load only when those files are being edited. What do you write?
cards.answer: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ use a `paths` field with glob patterns in YAML frontmatter, and they load only when Claude works with matching files. That cuts irrelevant context and tokens. A glob beats directory-level CLAUDE.md files when the files are spread across the codebase, and a skill is for on-demand workflows, not conventions.

choices.text: A `.claude/rules/` file with frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.tf"]` for all Terraform files
A `CLAUDE.md` inside each directory that contains Terraform files, describing the conventions
A project `CLAUDE.md` section that opens by naming the files it covers
A skill named terraform-conventions that developers invoke before editing those files

hints: Match the files by pattern, wherever they live.

cards.question: A codebase-analysis skill floods the main conversation with file listings before the real work starts. What fixes it?
cards.answer: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing skill outputs from polluting the main conversation. Compacting afterwards recovers space but the main session already spent it, and restricting tools does not make discovery quiet. Note: in current Claude Code docs, `allowed-tools` pre-approves the listed tools for that turn rather than restricting tools; use `disallowed-tools` or permission deny rules to restrict.

choices.text: Add `context: fork` so the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context
Add `allowed-tools` limiting the skill to Read so it produces less output overall
Move the skill body into a separate file that it reads only when needed
Run `/compact` after the skill finishes, reclaiming the space its output consumed

hints: Do not clean it up afterwards - have it happen somewhere else.

cards.question: You want a personal variant of a shared team skill. Teammates must not be affected, and you still want the team version too. How?
cards.answer: Personal skill customization means creating variants in ~/.claude/skills/ with different names, so teammates are not affected. Reusing the same name hides the team version from you, and editing the project skill changes or replaces the shared one. Note: current docs say a personal skill wins over a project skill with the same name.

choices.text: Create your variant in `~/.claude/skills/` under a different name
Create it in `~/.claude/skills/` with the same name, so yours wins
Edit the project skill, noting the change is your personal preference
Edit the project skill, but leave your change uncommitted locally

hints: Personal scope is half of it. The other half is the name.

cards.question: A stack trace points at one function and the fix is a missing null check. Plan mode or direct execution?
cards.answer: Direct execution is appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes - a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace is the guide's own example. Plan mode is for large-scale change, multiple valid approaches, and architectural decisions.

choices.text: Direct execution - the scope is clear and the change is contained
Plan mode, because any production fix deserves a reviewed plan first
Plan mode, since the null check may reveal other unguarded call sites
Direct execution, but only after Explore has mapped the calling code

hints: One file, one line, one clear cause.

cards.question: A multi-phase task keeps running out of context partway through its discovery phase. What prevents this?
cards.answer: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output and returns summaries, preserving the main conversation's context, which prevents context exhaustion in multi-phase tasks. Compacting after discovery comes too late: the context already ran out during it. Note: current docs say `allowed-tools` pre-approves tools rather than restricting them.

choices.text: The Explore subagent, which isolates discovery output and returns only summaries
Plan mode, which defers all file reading until the plan has been approved
A skill with `allowed-tools` restricted to Read, keeping the discovery narrow
Running `/compact` after discovery ends, before the implementation phase starts

hints: Have the noisy part happen in someone else's window.

cards.question: A prose description of a data transformation keeps being implemented slightly differently. What is the most effective fix?
cards.answer: Concrete input/output examples are named as the most effective way to communicate expected transformations when prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently. More prose - even better organized prose - is still prose.

choices.text: Provide two or three concrete input/output examples of the transformation
Rewrite the description as a numbered procedure with one action per step
Add the edge cases to the description, since they cause the drift
Ask for the implementation plan first, then correct it before any code

hints: Stop describing it and show it.

cards.question: You have five review findings, and fixing any one of them changes how the others should be fixed. How do you send them?
cards.answer: Interacting problems go in one message; independent problems are better fixed sequentially. Sequential iteration on interacting fixes means each one invalidates the previous.

choices.text: All five in a single detailed message, since the fixes interact
One at a time, verifying each fix before moving on to the next finding
Grouped by file, so each message keeps its changes locally consistent
Highest severity first, alone, then the remaining four together afterwards

hints: They interact. What does fixing one in isolation do to the others?

cards.question: A CI review re-runs after each new commit and the PR is filling with duplicate comments. What fixes it?
cards.answer: Including prior review findings in context and instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues is the named skill. Reviewing only the newest commit misses issues introduced by the interaction between commits.

choices.text: Include the prior findings and ask for only new or still-unaddressed issues
Delete the previous comments before each run so only the latest set remains
Run the review only on the newest commit's diff rather than the full branch
Deduplicate the findings in the posting step by comparing their text content

hints: The agent does not know what it already said unless you tell it.

cards.question: Generated tests keep duplicating scenarios the suite already covers. What is missing from the invocation?
cards.answer: Providing existing test files in context is what stops duplicate scenarios, and documenting testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md is what reduces low-value test output.

choices.text: The existing test files, plus documented fixtures and test criteria in CLAUDE.md
A higher turn limit, so the agent can read the suite before writing anything
A stricter prompt telling the agent not to duplicate any existing test case
A coverage report, so the agent writes tests only for the uncovered lines

hints: It cannot avoid what it has not seen.

cards.question: You built a skill that maps an unfamiliar module and prints hundreds of lines of findings. Developers report that after running it, the main conversation is cluttered and Claude starts losing track of the feature they were building. Which frontmatter option addresses this?
cards.answer: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context and returns only its result, so a verbose exploration never lands in the main conversation. `allowed-tools` limits which tools run, not how much they print. `argument-hint` narrows the input, not the transcript that comes back. Asking in the description for a summary is a prompt-level request with no guarantee.

choices.text: context: fork, so the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context and returns only its result.
allowed-tools, restricting the skill to read-only tools so it produces less output overall.
argument-hint, prompting the developer to narrow the scope before the skill runs.
A description that instructs Claude to summarize the skill output before it continues with the main conversation.

hints: The problem is what comes back into the transcript, not what the skill is allowed to touch.

cards.question: You maintain a monorepo where each package has its own maintainers and its own subset of relevant standards documents. You want each package's CLAUDE.md to pull in only the standards that apply to it, without duplicating text. Which mechanism fits?
cards.answer: `@import` lets each package's CLAUDE.md reference exactly the standards files that apply to it, so every standard keeps a single source of truth. Copying the sections into each package guarantees drift the moment one is edited. A root file holding every standard loads all of it and relies on inference to pick the right part. One skill per document turns always-on standards into a manual step.

choices.text: Use @import syntax in each package's CLAUDE.md to reference the specific standards files that apply.
Copy the relevant sections into each package's CLAUDE.md and keep them in sync during code review.
Put every standard in the root CLAUDE.md and let Claude infer which section applies to the current package.
Create one skill per standards document and ask developers to invoke the ones relevant to their package.

hints: Each standard should exist once and be composed per package.

cards.question: A skill in your repository generates migration files. During a dry run it deleted an unrelated file after misreading an instruction. You want a structural guarantee that this skill can only write new files, without rewriting the skill body. What do you configure?
cards.answer: `allowed-tools` restricts the tool surface available while the skill runs, which is the structural guarantee being asked for. `context: fork` isolates context, not permissions - a forked skill can still delete files. `argument-hint` only collects an argument. An instruction at the top of SKILL.md is prompt-based and probabilistic, which is exactly what already failed.

choices.text: The allowed-tools frontmatter field, limiting the skill to the file operations it legitimately needs.
The context: fork frontmatter field, so any destructive action happens in an isolated context.
The argument-hint frontmatter field, so the developer confirms the target path before execution.
A line at the top of SKILL.md instructing Claude never to delete or overwrite existing files.

hints: A structural guarantee lives in the tool surface, not in the prompt.

cards.question: The shared .claude/skills/generate-tests skill suits the team, but you personally want a variant that also writes property-based tests. You must not change how the skill behaves for teammates. What do you do?
cards.answer: A personal variant belongs in `~/.claude/skills/` under a **different name**, so it is visible only in your sessions and the shared skill keeps working untouched for everyone. Same-name shadowing also stays local but makes it ambiguous which skill actually ran. Editing the project skill changes a shared artifact for one person's preference. A long-lived branch is a permanent merge burden.

choices.text: Create your variant under ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name so only your sessions see it.
Edit the project skill and add a flag that teammates can leave unset to keep the old behavior.
Copy the project skill to a branch and rebase it onto main whenever the shared version changes.
Override the project skill with a file of the same name in ~/.claude/skills/ so yours wins locally.

hints: User scope is private, but a name collision is not the same as a separate skill.
